Rahguzar Commute Networks: Whose k Is It?

A case on virality and the viral coefficient

1. Sunday night, Hoshangabad Road

At a quarter past nine on Sunday, 4 October 2026, Malini Sisodiya sat alone on the second floor of Rahguzar Commute Networks' office on Hoshangabad Road, Bhopal, with two versions of one slide open. The first, circulated by the chief executive, read "Virality: k up by half in a quarter" above a line rising from 0.410 in June to 0.620 in September. The second showed eleven viral coefficients for the same corridors in the same month, from 0.118 to 2.380.

The board met at eleven the next morning at Vindhya Growth Partners' office in Gurugram. Of a ₹90 crore Series B, ₹54 crore had come in; ₹36 crore was held as a tranche releasable on "a viral coefficient of at least 0.55 sustained over two consecutive quarters". Nobody had written down which viral coefficient.

Malini had joined in 2023 as Rahguzar's first product manager and now ran product and growth. Nine days inside the invite funnel had turned up no error: every figure in the pack was computed correctly. They were simply not the same figure, and the one chosen was the largest.

2. Company history, and a decision that saved ₹18 lakh

Brijesh Chouhan founded Rahguzar in January 2021 after eleven years at an auto-components plant at Mandideep, watching four-seat cars carry one person each down NH-46. The mechanic is narrow: a rider posts a corridor and a time, a driver with spare seats accepts, and the app prices the seat as a fuel-and-toll share.

By September 2026 there were 28,40,000 installs, 19,60,000 registered riders, 2,74,000 monthly active riders and 11,60,000 seat bookings in the month at an average take of ₹14 a seat, or ₹1.62 crore of revenue. FY26 revenue was ₹19.4 crore against a ₹12.6 crore loss; cash was ₹28 crore and net burn ₹1.4 crore a month, or twenty months.

The decision that shaped everything was taken in March 2025 and looked like housekeeping. Rather than buy a mobile measurement partner, Rahguzar built attribution in-house on a last-touch rule and cut retention of raw invite and install events from 400 days to 45, saving ₹18 lakh a year. Nothing older than forty-five days can be recomputed, so no definition reaches back across a quarter; and last touch credits a rider signed up at an office-park desk to whichever colleague's link they tapped on the way in.

Sawaari Credits, launched in October 2025, pays ₹40 of seat credit per accepted invite. Hamraah Invite, shipped in June 2026, pre-fills an invitation with the sender's own corridor and departure window.

3. The industry

Ola, Uber and BluSmart sell a car and a driver; Rahguzar sells an empty seat in a colleague's car. Quick Ride and sRide share one structural fact: a carpool is worthless until two strangers want the same road at the same hour, so the unit of value is a corridor.

Pooling in a white-plate private car sits under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and the Motor Vehicles Aggregators Guidelines, 2020, and state transport departments cap a car's pooled trips per day. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 bears on the growth engine directly: an invite that uploads a colleague's number processes that colleague's personal data, and Rahguzar's consent flow was written in 2023.

Global exposure ran through eleven corporate contracts. The largest, ₹1.84 crore a year, was with Kandelberg Precision Group, a Zurich engineering firm whose 3,600-seat capability centre sits at Mandideep. Kandelberg buys verified carpool seats as a commute benefit and counts the avoided vehicle-kilometres in its sustainability report, so its auditors own the definition of an active rider in clause 7: eight or more paid seats a month. Elena Furrer, its head of workplace mobility, budgeted for 1,200 such riders a month.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

June 2026. Hamraah Invite shipped. A two-week experiment on the Bhopal and Gwalior corridors read it at plus 0.041 on k, on a fourteen-day window with the accepted event set to a registration that had saved a home corridor. Reported June k: 0.410. Rachna Jadon, running the test from Tallinn, flagged that the read was within a corridor and over two weeks. The flag did not travel.

July. The window widened from fourteen days to thirty, because commuters change arrangements at the start of a month. It applied to July onwards; May's raw events had aged past forty-five days.

August. A driver-app release made the first-ride-completed event unreliable for nine days, and an analyst moved the accepted event to plain registration. The change was correct, sat in a commit message, and was never announced.

September. ₹24.80 lakh of a ₹69.40 lakh growth budget went into a new Gurugram corridor, the densest office catchment the company had entered. Reported k: 0.620. On the Kandelberg campus: 1.150, set in bold.

Three things have turned out to be wrong, and none is a bug. Exhibit 6 shows the rise to 0.620 is almost all accounting and mix; Exhibit 5 dissolves the campus figure; Exhibit 1 shows the numerator alone moves k about fifteenfold, and about twentyfold once row 11's different denominator is admitted.

Figure A: the measurement timeline, ordered, not to scale.

5. The people

Malini Sisodiya, vice-president, product and growth, Bhopal. Position: stop reporting one company-wide k. Incentive: Vikrant Saraf has twice praised her board reporting. Not saying: she approved the July window change herself, in four words in a Slack thread.

Brijesh Chouhan, co-founder and chief executive, Bhopal. Position: the tranche keeps twenty months of runway from becoming twelve, and a definitional argument in a board meeting is how founders lose rounds. Not saying: he has told two hires the round is closed.

Vandita Parmar, head of growth marketing, Bhopal. Position: 0.620, on a thirty-day window and registration basis, is the standard read. Incentive: her variable pay is set on invite-sourced registrations. Not saying: the August change lifted her own number.

Ritvik Namdeo, vice-president, finance, Bhopal. Position: k must be organic, so anything paid for leaves the numerator and the denominator is every rider who could invite. His figure is 0.118. Not saying: at 0.118 no window clears the milestone.

Bhoomika Tomar, city operations lead, Raipur. Position: a registration is not a rider; one who never books makes her matching worse, because the app shows drivers demand that is not there. Her figure is 0.248. Not saying: she has stopped using the company k.

Rachna Jadon, lead data scientist, Tallinn. Position: all eleven numbers in Exhibit 1 are correct and none is k, because the quantity the board believes in is not identified by the data the company holds. Not saying: her own June read does not survive.

Vikrant Saraf, partner, Vindhya Growth Partners, Gurugram. Position: the install-based 0.790 is what his comparables use, and the campus figure above one proves the model works somewhere. Incentive: he wants the tranche released, and sits on the committee that will ask why the milestone was drafted loosely. Not saying: his fund's mid-year letter cites the campus figure.

— Rachna Jadon, memo, 28 September

— Ritvik Namdeo, email, 2 October

8. The options as Malini currently sees them

A: present 0.620 and footnote the basis. Defensible, standard, and it clears 0.55. It needs a trend line whose June point sits on a different basis from its September, the difference in a footnote nobody reads aloud.

B: restate to the strictest basis. Report 0.155 on paying riders and ask the board to replace a milestone written on a quantity nobody could then measure. Honest, and it gives Vindhya's committee a reason to reprice the round.

C: publish a measurement charter. Pre-register one definition, report it per corridor, drop the company figure. Two engineers for seven weeks — the whole driver-supply roadmap — and no month before July is recovered.

D: spend into Gurugram. The ₹2.10 crore Q3 budget, put where corridor k is highest, would lift the company figure without changing any corridor's performance, as Exhibit 4 shows. It is the only option that moves the reported number by the deadline.

All four accept that a single scalar called k is what a board should govern by. Malini had begun to suspect this was the assumption doing the damage — that what she should defend was a per-corridor seat-fill and a payback, and that the tranche condition was the artefact. She also knew the cost of telling a board the metric is wrong four days after circulating a slide celebrating it.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at eleven on Monday, 5 October 2026. The ₹36 crore tranche requires k of at least 0.55 for two consecutive quarters and names no window, numerator or denominator; on the reported basis the company has one such quarter, on the June basis none. Cash is ₹28 crore against ₹1.4 crore a month of burn. The Q3 FY27 growth budget is ₹2.10 crore, or ₹70 lakh a month, level with September's ₹69.40 lakh. Engineering is nine people under a freeze, raw events are kept forty-five days, legal's DPDP note is due 9 October, and Kandelberg renews on 31 December.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, name the row you would call the viral coefficient, and what a reader may conclude from it that the others do not.
  2. Exhibit 2 moves k by 0.248 on the window alone, against 0.041 for the year's largest product change. What should a team do with a metric more sensitive to its accounting than to its product?
  3. Exhibit 3 puts ₹31.00 lakh of September's ₹69.40 lakh arguably inside the "organic" numerator. Is a paid-for invite organic? Argue both treatments and say what would settle it.
  4. If a company k is a spend-weighted average across corridors of unequal route density, what is the smallest unit at which virality can honestly be reported, and what does a board lose by governing there?
  5. Exhibit 5 unwinds a figure above one to 0.797, then 0.360, then 0.100, and Vikrant Saraf's fund has cited the first. What does Malini owe him, Brijesh Chouhan and Vindhya's investors, in what order?
  6. It is Monday morning. What goes on the screen at eleven, what does she say when Vikrant Saraf asks whether the milestone is met, and what should the tranche condition measure instead, knowing she cannot recompute a month before July?

She saved both versions and deleted neither. Outside, the last Mandideep shift traffic headed south, four seats to a car, one person in each.

Virality and the Viral Coefficient

How does a product spread from customer to customer — and how much of that spread can a team actually plan for, measure, and defend in front of a board?

1. A number Meera has to defend in six weeks

On the second Monday of January 2026, Meera Kulkarni, Head of Growth at Vasundhara Play, a Bengaluru-based casual social-gaming app, opened her performance-marketing dashboard and did the arithmetic she had been avoiding since December. Vasundhara Play was paying an average of ₹182 to acquire an installed, activated user through Meta and Google campaigns, up from ₹121 fourteen months earlier as auction prices in the Indian gaming-app category climbed. The company had 2.3 million monthly active users, was burning roughly ₹3.1 crore a month, and had eleven months of runway left. The board had scheduled a Series B readiness review for the last week of February, and the one question every partner in the room would ask was the same one Meera's own CFO had already asked twice: what, other than more rupees into Meta's auction, was going to bring blended CAC down before the fundraising conversation started.

Meera's answer, sketched on a whiteboard that Monday afternoon, was a referral mechanic: after a player finished a match, the app would offer a one-tap share of the result to WhatsApp contacts, with a small reward — in-app coins, not cash — for both the sender and anyone who joined and played a match within 48 hours. It was a two-week engineering build, competing directly against a roadmap slot her product lead wanted for a new game mode. To win that slot, and to walk into the board meeting with something more credible than a hunch, Meera needed to translate "people will share this" into a number precise enough to argue with: the viral coefficient, usually written as K. Get the estimate wrong in either direction — oversell it to the board and under-deliver, or underestimate it and lose the engineering slot to a feature that won't move CAC at all — and she loses either the fundraise's credibility or six weeks she doesn't have.

2. The idea, stated plainly

The viral coefficient, K, is the average number of new customers that each existing customer generates through the product's own invitation or sharing mechanism, before any paid or organic channel is counted. It answers a narrower question than "does this product spread by word of mouth," which is really a question about human behaviour outside anyone's control. K answers the product-management version of that question: of the invitations a specific in-product mechanic causes people to send, how many convert into new, activated users, and does that multiply fast enough to matter.

The vocabulary has two separate parents. The phrase "viral marketing" was coined in 1997 by the venture capitalists Tim Draper and Steve Jurvetson at Draper Fisher Jurvetson, describing what they had just watched happen at Hotmail: in 1996, Hotmail's founders appended the line "PS: I love you. Get your free email at Hotmail" to the bottom of every outgoing message, and the service went from zero to twelve million users in eighteen months without a meaningful marketing budget. The formal coefficient — a single number a team could forecast, target, and defend in a board deck the way Meera needed to — came later, popularised through the late 2000s by growth-stage investors, most visibly David Skok at Matrix Partners, who borrowed the underlying logic from epidemiology's basic reproduction number, the average number of new infections one infected person causes in a susceptible population. A product with K above 1 behaves, mathematically, like an outbreak: growth compounds without new fuel. A product with K below 1 behaves like an outbreak that burns out: it still adds users, but the additions decay generation by generation toward zero.

The sentence Meera could say in the boardroom without sounding glib: "K tells you how many additional users each existing user brings in through the invite mechanism itself — it's a multiplier on top of whatever we already pay to acquire, not a replacement for it."

3. The mechanics, one step at a time

Four steps happen inside that loop, and practitioners routinely skip past two of them when they talk about "our K." First, an existing user has to be exposed to an invitation surface at a moment when sharing feels natural — Vasundhara Play chose the instant after a match ends, when the player has just seen a score worth showing off, rather than a generic "invite friends" button buried in a settings menu that almost nobody opens. Second, that user sends some number of invitations; averaged across every existing user, including the majority who send none at all, this is i. Third, each invitation has to be delivered, opened, and acted upon by the recipient, who must not just install the app but cross whatever bar the team has defined as "activated" — for Vasundhara Play, playing one full match, not merely opening the app once; the fraction of invitations that clear this bar is c. Fourth, and this is the step most dashboards quietly drop, that newly activated user needs time to become, in turn, an existing user who might send invitations of their own — the cycle time, T. K is simply i multiplied by c; it says nothing on its own about how quickly that multiplication happens in the calendar, which is why two products with an identical K can grow at very different real-world speeds.

4. The arithmetic, worked twice

Meera's data team pulled two numbers from a four-week pilot run with 1,000 seed users who had already been activated through paid channels. On average, each of those 1,000 users sent 2.5 invitations through the new share sheet (i = 2.5), and 8% of invitations sent resulted in a new, activated user within the 48-hour reward window (c = 0.08). That gives a viral coefficient of K = 2.5 × 0.08 = 0.2. Because K is below 1, the seed cohort's viral descendants form a decaying series: generation one contributes 1,000 × 0.2 = 200 new users; generation two contributes 200 × 0.2 = 40; generation three, 8; generation four, roughly 2; and so on, each generation one-fifth the size of the one before it. Summed to infinity, a decaying geometric series like this converges to seed × K ÷ (1−K), so the 1,000 seed users eventually generate about 1,000 × 0.2/0.8 = 250 additional users through the loop alone, for a final cohort of roughly 1,250 — a real but modest 25% uplift on the original paid spend, not a replacement for it.

Meera's second pass changed one input. Her design lead proposed making the reward two-sided and more visible — both sender and receiver get 500 coins, shown as an animated banner rather than a line of text — and a small test suggested this would lift conversion from 8% to 15%, without materially changing how many invitations people sent. Holding i at 2.5 and raising c to 0.15 gives K = 2.5 × 0.15 = 0.375. The same seed of 1,000 users now yields 1,000 × 0.375/0.625 ≈ 600 additional users, for a cohort of roughly 1,600 — nearly triple the uplift of the first design, from a change that touched only the reward's visibility and size, not the underlying sharing behaviour at all. The table below runs both scenarios generation by generation, alongside a third, more aggressive scenario the team modelled but did not build: an even lower-friction one-tap WhatsApp share (raising i to 5) combined with the improved reward (c = 0.22), which pushes K to 1.1 — just over the threshold where growth stops decaying and starts compounding.

The qualitative lesson Meera took from the table was not "chase K past 1" — her honest estimate for the one-tap design was closer to 1.1 under optimistic assumptions and likely lower once fatigue set in, and she did not trust it enough to put in front of the board. It was that the visible-reward redesign, a comparatively cheap change, nearly tripled the return on every paid user she was already buying, and that this held even in the conservative, sub-1 case. Cycle time mattered too: the pilot's loop closed in about nine days on average, meaning even the 250-user uplift from the first design took most of a month to materialise, a timeline she needed to build into the board narrative rather than imply the referral mechanic would show results the week it shipped.

5. What a learner needs to get past the vocabulary

The averaging trap in "i"

K is only meaningful when i is averaged across every existing user exposed to the mechanism, including the overwhelming majority who send no invitations at all. Teams that instead compute i only among people who used the share feature — "our sharers send 6 invites each!" — produce a number several times too high, because it silently drops the denominator of non-sharers. The two numbers answer different questions: the second describes an engaged minority's behaviour, which is a useful segmentation fact, but only the first feeds correctly into a forecast of total new users.

Word of mouth is not the same thing as a measured K

People telling a friend about Vasundhara Play over chai, with no in-product mechanism involved, is real virality and genuinely drives installs, but it is invisible to a K computed from a specific invite feature's telemetry. Conflating "total organic growth" with "the referral feature's K" runs in both directions: it can make a mediocre feature look responsible for growth that was happening anyway, or make total viral spread look smaller than it is because the informal, unmeasured channel is larger than the engineered one.

Virality is not the same idea as a network effect

A network effect describes value: the product gets more useful to each user as more users join, the way a messaging app or a marketplace does. Virality describes a mechanism of acquisition: how a new user shows up. The two often travel together but are logically separate — a horoscope app can have a high K purely from curiosity-sharing despite having no network effect at all, while a product with a powerful network effect can still have a mediocre engineered K if nobody bothered to build a good invite surface.

Durable K above 1 is close to mythical

Hotmail, early PayPal, and Dropbox in specific windows are the examples every deck cites precisely because sustained K above 1 is rare enough to be famous. Most mature consumer products that report a "healthy" K are living somewhere between 0.1 and 0.4 for long stretches, and that range is still commercially valuable — not because it replaces paid or organic acquisition, but because it quietly and permanently lowers the blended cost of every user the company buys.

Cycle time is as decisive as the coefficient itself

Two loops with an identical K of 0.3 but cycle times of three days and thirty days reach the same eventual multiplier, but one gets there in a fortnight and the other in the better part of a year. A team evaluating a referral redesign against a fundraising deadline, as Meera was, has to weight cycle time at least as heavily as the headline K, because a mathematically superior loop that closes too slowly may deliver nothing the board can see by February.

K says nothing about the quality of who arrives

A viral loop that pays both sender and receiver in coins or cash risks attracting reward-seekers rather than genuine players, and a K of 0.3 built on an incentivised loop can carry materially worse day-30 retention than the same headline number built on unprompted sharing. K must always be read alongside a cohort retention or LTV comparison against paid and organic users from the same period; on its own it is silent on whether the users it produces are worth having.

Measured K usually overstates true incrementality

Referral-link attribution is generous by construction: it credits the loop with any install carrying a referral code, including people who would have found the app anyway — through search, through an ad they'd already seen, through a friend mentioning it verbally and the link just being the easiest way to click through. The clean way to find true incremental K is a holdout: turn the invite surface off for a comparable slice of users or cities and compare organic install rates against a matched control, which almost no team does because it costs a few weeks of "foregone" growth to run.

Saturation quietly erodes K over the product's life

As an existing user's pool of contacts who don't already have the app shrinks — because the product has already spread through their social graph — the same invite mechanism converts fewer of the invitations it still sends, and c drifts down even with no change to the feature itself. A K measured in the first month a referral feature ships describes that month, not a stable long-run constant, and re-measuring it quarterly is not optional.

6. How the loop changes shape by product type and by stage

In a consumer product like Vasundhara Play, virality is often casual-contact virality: the product itself generates a naturally shareable artifact — a score, a streak, a result — and India's WhatsApp-native sharing culture means i tends to start higher than in markets where messaging is more fragmented. The highest-leverage changes Meera's team found were about removing friction — a native share sheet, a prefilled message, one tap instead of three — rather than raising the incentive, which is consistent with what the arithmetic in Figure 2 already showed: moving c mattered more than the incentive's cost implied it should.

In a B2B product, the shape is different in kind, not just in degree. Consider a contemporary in a different Indian city: Viren Works, a project-management SaaS out of Pune selling to mid-market operations teams. Its "invite" is not a marketing prompt at all — it is a colleague being added to a workspace so a task can be assigned or a document reviewed, which is to say the invite is core product usage, not a bolt-on growth feature. i and c there are governed by how essential collaboration is to the underlying workflow rather than by copy or incentive design, and a buying committee — IT approval, a procurement cycle, a security review — can slow or block seat-level viral growth in ways a consumer gaming app never encounters. Slack and Dropbox are the textbook examples of this account-expansion virality in the broader market, and it is exactly the mechanism the case this topic unlocks, the Dropbox case, is built around.

In a marketplace, virality is two-sided and asymmetric, and the two sides should almost never be tracked as one blended K. Picture Vaishali Mandi, a business-to-business-to-consumer marketplace connecting wholesale produce traders in Punjab and Haryana mandis to kirana retailers in nearby towns. A trader who invites other traders does so because more traders on the platform means deeper liquidity for everyone — a loop reinforced by the marketplace's own network effect. A retailer who invites another retailer does so mainly because of a referral credit, a loop that behaves much more like Vasundhara Play's coin-based mechanic. Because the two sides of a marketplace are rarely in equal supply, a referral on the thinner side — usually the supply side, the traders — is worth disproportionately more to overall liquidity than the same referral on the thicker side, and a single blended K obscures exactly the decision that matters: which side to spend the growth budget engineering a loop for.

Stage changes the calculus again. Early-stage, with a seed cohort as small as Meera's 1,000 users, K is statistically noisy — a handful of unusually enthusiastic sharers can swing the whole estimate, and "activation" itself may still be loosely defined, making c unreliable in either direction. But this is also precisely when a promising K is most valuable strategically, because paid CAC is least affordable relative to the funding a young company actually has. Late-stage, at tens of millions of users, K becomes statistically stable but structurally declines — saturation, invite fatigue, and a shrinking pool of not-yet-reached contacts all push it down over time — yet even a modest K of 0.05 to 0.1 is worth tens of crores a year in avoided ad spend purely because of the volume it is multiplying. The question a late-stage team should ask is not "is our K exciting" but "is this K, net of incentive cost, still compounding a meaningful CAC saving at our current scale."

7. Where teams go wrong

The first and most common mistake is counting gross referral-attributed installs as free growth without ever running a holdout. The symptom is visible on almost every growth dashboard that reports this way: a chart of "referred installs" climbing nicely month over month, while blended CAC and paid channel spend barely move at all. The underlying misunderstanding is treating a generous attribution rule — any install carrying a referral code gets credited to the loop — as proof that the install would not have happened otherwise. The cheapest diagnostic is a randomized or geo-based holdout: switch the invite surface off for a comparable segment or city for a few weeks and compare organic install rates against the group that still has it.

The second mistake is reporting a single blended K and treating it as descriptive of the typical user. The symptom is a leadership team celebrating "K = 0.3" on the strength of one dashboard number, while the actual growth curve refuses to behave the way that number predicts. The misunderstanding is statistical: a mean drawn from a power-law distribution, where a tiny fraction of users generate most of the invitations, doesn't describe what a representative user does and can be knocked around by a single campaign or a single unusually active cohort. The diagnostic is cheap — plot the distribution of invites sent per user, not just its average, and recompute K with the top one percent of senders excluded to see how much of the number they're carrying.

The third mistake is chasing K past 1.0 as if it were the goal rather than one input among several. The symptom is a team endlessly iterating on invite copy and incentive size for a marginal K improvement while cycle time and unit economics go unexamined. The misunderstanding is treating K as a vanity metric instead of feeding it into a model that also accounts for how fast the loop closes and how much each converted invitation costs to reward. The diagnostic is to compute a fully loaded cost per viral user — total incentive spend divided by converted invitations — and compare it honestly against paid CAC; a K of 0.25 achieved cheaply frequently beats a K of 0.5 propped up by an expensive reward.

The fourth mistake is launching an incentivised referral programme with no retention or fraud check built in from day one. The symptom is a visible spike in referral-attributed signups that fails to retain past day three, alongside a finance team quietly flagging an unexpectedly large wallet-credit or gift-card liability. The underlying misunderstanding is assuming that an incentivised invite carries the same downstream quality as an unprompted one. The diagnostic is to compare day-seven retention and early LTV of the referred cohort against the organic cohort from the same week; when the referred cohort retains materially worse, the loop is manufacturing installs rather than manufacturing customers.

8. What the decision looks like handled well

Handled well, this is what Meera's next six weeks look like. She ships the visible, two-sided reward redesign — the c = 0.15 version, not the untested one-tap design she couldn't yet trust — to a clean 10% holdout split rather than to everyone at once, so that in three weeks she has an incremental, not just an attributed, number to show the board. She reports K by segment, not as one blended figure, flagging that the top 5% of sharers are carrying more than half of all invitations sent, and treats that as a targeting opportunity rather than hiding it inside an average. She tracks cycle time alongside K from week one, so the board narrative says "this adds roughly 250 to 600 incremental users per thousand paid users, arriving over three to four weeks" rather than implying an overnight step-change. And she prices the coin reward into a fully loaded cost per viral user, which she can set directly against the ₹182 paid CAC, making the case not as "virality replaces paid marketing" but as "this lowers our blended CAC by a specific, defensible amount while paid spend keeps doing the heavier lifting." That is a materially smaller claim than "we found a growth engine," and a much more fundable one.

9. What Meera decides, and what to sit with next

Meera takes the roadmap slot, ships the visible-reward version behind a holdout, and walks into the February board meeting with a number she can defend rather than a number she hopes survives scrutiny: an estimated 20–35% reduction in blended CAC over the following two quarters, sourced to a measured, incremental K rather than to gross referral-attributed installs, with the caveat that the figure will erode as the city's WhatsApp-connected player base gets progressively more saturated and needs re-measuring every quarter rather than assumed. She does not promise the board a viral growth engine, because the arithmetic in front of her never supported that claim; she promises a multiplier on the paid spend the company was already committing to, at a cost she can price. The next topic that follows naturally from here, and the one this page's own graph points to, is referral-programme design itself — the mechanics of reward structure, fraud control, and invite-surface placement that turn a K estimate like Meera's from a whiteboard sketch into a shipped feature; the Dropbox case, built on the same coefficient but at a company where K briefly exceeded 1, is the natural next stop after that, precisely because it shows what changes, and what stays dangerously the same, when the rare case actually happens.

Question one: if a team can only measure K accurately through a holdout it hasn't yet run, what should it be willing to say about virality — to a board, to itself — before that holdout exists?

Question two: at what point does a shrinking, saturating K stop being a growth lever worth re-measuring quarterly and become a number a company should simply stop reporting on its own?

Vasundhara Play, Viren Works, and Vaishali Mandi are illustrative composites used for teaching purposes and are not real companies. Figures are constructed to demonstrate the underlying arithmetic of viral-coefficient forecasting.

Phailaav Classifieds: The Diwali Share Decision

A case on virality and the viral coefficient

1. Opening

On the evening of Tuesday, 29 September 2026, Naveen Rangasamy, head of growth at Phailaav Classifieds, sat in the fourth-floor office on Avinashi Road, Coimbatore, with a single chart open on his laptop. It showed the number of new users the company's "share to your building group" button had produced in each of the last four months. The line only went down.

Diwali fell on 8 November, and Dhanteras two days earlier. The weeks before Diwali were the busiest of the year for second-hand sofas, refrigerators and school cycles. Gowri Velayudham, the chief executive, had asked Naveen for one recommendation by Friday, 2 October: how should the company spend the single growth push it could afford before the festival?

2. Company background

Phailaav Classifieds was founded in 2021 by Gowri and two college friends. The app lets people in tier-2 towns list used goods and local services (electricians, tutors, tiffin makers), chat with buyers and sellers, and, since late 2023, tap "Jhonka Share" to post a listing straight into their apartment building's WhatsApp group. By September 2026 it had 14,00,000 monthly active users across 38 towns in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Kerala. Revenue in FY26 was ₹11.4 crore, mostly from promoted listings and lead fees from service providers, against a loss of ₹7.2 crore. Cash stood at ₹22 crore and monthly burn at ₹1.2 crore, about 18 months of runway.

OLX India and Quikr were the established general classifieds; Facebook Marketplace and neighbourhood WhatsApp groups took much of the informal trade; Justdial and Urban Company served local services; Phailaav's argument was hyperlocal trust, and it was also its growth engine. Paid installs in tier-2 towns cost ₹125 each on Google and Meta, so most growth had to come from users bringing others.

3. The situation

The viral coefficient, k, is the number of new users each new user brings in. It is invitations per user multiplied by the share that convert. Phailaav's data scientist, Oviya Palanivel, who works from Sydney and joins the growth stand-up at 6:30 a.m. India time, measured k monthly by tracing every install back to a shared link. If k is below 1, each cohort produces a shrinking echo; the total number of users a cohort ultimately generates is its size multiplied by 1/(1 − k).

Exhibit 1 shows what Oviya found for September. Of 1,00,000 new users, 22 per cent shared at least one listing to a building group, an average of 3 shares each. Each share was seen by about 25 people who were not yet on Phailaav, and 1.2 per cent of those viewers installed the app. That produced 19,800 installs, a k of 0.198.

The team saw the problem from different places. 4. The people

Gowri Velayudham, chief executive, Coimbatore. She wants a visible jump in monthly users before the next fundraise in January, but has said she will not trade product quality for it.

Oviya Palanivel, data scientist, Sydney. She wants the company to fix what it measures: installs are not users, and k measured on installs flatters everything.

Girija Chinnadurai, design lead, Amsterdam. She wants the link to open a listing page in the browser, with no forced install, and thinks any reward will turn group chats into spam.

5. The options

Naveen had three courses of action, each of which Oviya modelled on the September cohort of 1,00,000 users. Exhibit 3 sets them beside the status quo on a single basis: every count is for that one cohort, the entire one-time cost is charged to it, and cost per user is total cost divided by the users in the row.

Option A: Chingari Credits. Pay ₹50 of promoted-listing credit to the sharer and ₹50 to the new joiner for every joiner who activates, meaning lists or chats within seven days. It takes a week to build, at ₹6,00,000. Oviya expects the sharing rate to rise to 30 per cent and the install rate to 1.5 per cent. That makes 30,000 sharers, 90,000 shares, 22,50,000 views and 33,750 installs, a k of 0.338. But reward-seekers activate less often: 30 per cent, against 45 per cent today.

Option B: Fix the landing. Shared links open a full listing page in the browser, with a chat prompt asking for the app only at reply. 6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, explain in your own words why k is 0.198. Which of its factors (sharers, shares, views, install rate) does each option try to move?
  2. Exhibit 2 shows k falling from 0.310 to 0.198 while the cohort shrank by one-sixth. What does saturation in a building group imply for the ceiling on k, and can any option lift it?
  3. Why does Option A's higher k fail to produce more day-30 users? What does that say about counting installs rather than retained users?
  4. If you were Naveen, which option would you take to Gowri on Friday, and what would you tell Wilson, whose city teams want rewards?

7. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. Virality is not a feeling that a product "spreads". It is a chain of measurable steps, and k is the product of the steps. A team that can name the weakest step can put money where it matters. Here the weakest step is the last: of 16,50,000 people who saw a listing, only 1.2 per cent installed. Reward programmes tend to push on the first steps (more sharing) and to admit the wrong people at the end; that is why Option A's k rises while its retained users fall.

A defensible path. Take Option B, and ship it on 30 October. It has the best cost per activated user (₹153) and per day-30 user (₹383), it lifts day-30 users from 3,564 to 6,270, a rise of 76 per cent, and it keeps Girija's promise that group chats will not fill with paid-for spam. The k of 0.314 is nearer to 1 than 0.198 but still well below it, so it will not make the company self-sustaining; it makes each rupee of future effort work harder. Wilson's concern deserves a small capped credits pilot in one town after Diwali, judged on day-30 users. Skip Option C: it is the costliest per day-30 user and leaves the funnel unchanged.

The residual risk is the calendar. Naveen should agree a cut-line in advance (browser listing page first, chat prompt second) so a partial fix still ships before Dhanteras.
