Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation · Growth & Retention · Near-expert depth

Virality and the Viral Coefficient

Two teams, two arguments about the same number: one cannot agree what a viral conversion is, the other cannot explain why theirs halved without anyone touching the feature. Both arguments have the same root — the viral coefficient is not a property of a product, but of a product meeting a particular graph at a particular moment.

1. Two rooms, three weeks apart

On Friday, 6 February 2026, in a glass-walled room on the fourth floor of an office block in Hyderabad's Financial District, Kavya Raghunathan, VP Product at Jaideep Systems, watched two of her own analysts present mutually incompatible numbers for the same thing. Jaideep Systems sells a document-approval and signature workflow to mid-market Indian firms — non-banking financial companies chasing loan files, third-party logistics operators chasing proof-of-delivery, hospital groups chasing insurer pre-authorisations. It had 2,600 paying workspaces, ₹41 crore of ARR, and a sales-assisted cost of ₹1.9 lakh to land a new logo, against a payback period the board had just described, in writing, as "structurally too long."

The disputed number concerned the product's external-reviewer flow. When a Jaideep customer sends a document out for approval, the counterparty — a vendor, a branch manager at another firm, an insurer's medical officer — receives a link and can review and sign without creating any account at all. Tanmay Pillai, a growth analyst working out of Chennai, had put the account-level viral coefficient of that surface at 0.34. Sunayana Deb, from the finance-analytics team two desks away, had put it at 0.04. Neither had made an arithmetic error. Tanmay had looked at every external counterparty touched in the preceding twelve months and asked whether that counterparty's employer had become a Jaideep customer by any route; Sunayana had looked at a ninety-day window, counted only self-serve workspaces created with an intact referral token, and excluded anything a salesperson had touched. The decision riding on the gap was an eleven-week engineering programme to require counterparties to create a free Jaideep identity before signing — the mechanism that turned Dropbox and Slack into distribution systems for themselves — against the objection from Jaideep's sales leadership that friction on the counterparty's side would cost the company the one thing its customers actually bought it for: documents that come back signed.

Nineteen days later and 950 kilometres north-west, in Indore, Anirudh Bhatia, Head of Growth at Jeevika Learning, was staring at a different pathology. Jeevika sells Hindi- and Marathi-first preparation for state public-service, staff-selection and banking examinations: 6.8 million installs, 940,000 monthly actives, a ₹1,499 annual subscription taken up by 3.1% of actives, and a paid acquisition cost of ₹214 per activated user in a Meta and Google auction that had grown 40% more expensive in eighteen months. Jeevika's growth had, for two years, been carried by a study-group invite loop: an aspirant preparing for, say, the MPSC preliminary examination could create a study group and pull classmates in from WhatsApp. In the quarter ending September 2025 that loop had measured a viral coefficient of 0.52. In the quarter ending March 2026 it measured 0.21. No one had shipped a change to it. Anirudh's CFO, Rohit Sabharwal, had frozen ₹6.4 crore of annual referral incentive pending an explanation, and the explanation on offer from Anirudh's own team — "the feature has got stale, we should rebuild it" — was, he suspected, exactly wrong.

The two rooms were arguing about opposite ends of the same misconception. Kavya's team believed the viral coefficient was a fact awaiting correct measurement; Anirudh's believed it was a property of their feature that had degraded. It is neither. K is a measurement of an interaction between a product mechanism and a specific social graph at a specific level of penetration, over a specific window, against a specific counterfactual. Change any of those four and the number changes without the product changing at all. Everything that follows — the arithmetic, the edge cases, the failure modes, the live disagreements in the field — is downstream of taking that sentence seriously.

2. The idea, its history, and the four camps that will not agree about it

State the definition tightly, because the looseness is where the damage starts. The viral coefficient, K, is the expected number of additional activated users produced, through the product's own invitation or artefact mechanism, by one activated user, over a defined observation window, net of the users who would have arrived anyway. Four qualifiers are doing real work there, and practitioners routinely drop three of them: per which population (all actives, or only those exposed to the surface?), over what window (ninety days, or a lifetime?), at what activation bar (installed, or performed the core action?), and net of what counterfactual (gross attributed, or incremental against a holdout?). Kavya's 0.34 and 0.04 differ on three of the four. They are not a measurement dispute; they are a definition dispute wearing a measurement's clothes.

The vocabulary has two distinct parents. "Viral marketing" was named in 1997 by Steve Jurvetson and Tim Draper of Draper Fisher Jurvetson, describing what they had watched at Hotmail, where a single line appended to every outgoing message — "PS: I love you. Get your free email at Hotmail" — carried the service to roughly twelve million users in eighteen months on a negligible media budget. The coefficient itself was borrowed later, and from elsewhere: from the basic reproduction number of epidemiology, formalised in the Kermack–McKendrick compartmental models of 1927, and behind that from the Galton–Watson branching process of the 1870s, invented to ask whether aristocratic surnames would die out. Through the late 2000s and 2010s that borrowing was popularised for operators — by Adam Penenberg's taxonomy of viral loops, by David Skok's widely copied treatment of viral coefficient and viral cycle time, by Andrew Chen's observation that every acquisition channel decays as it is exploited, and by the growth-engineering movement Sean Ellis named. The problem it was invented to solve was mundane and financial: distribution had become the scarce input, word of mouth was the cheapest distribution there was, and no one could put word of mouth into a plan. K made it a line item. That was its enormous virtue and remains its central risk.

Four camps now hold genuinely different positions, and an experienced product leader refereeing an argument between two competent practitioners should be able to name which camp each is speaking from.

The coefficient school — the operator tradition running from Skok and Penenberg through most growth-team practice — holds that a well-instrumented invite surface produces a number stable enough over a quarter to forecast from, and that product changes move it predictably enough to justify a roadmap slot. It will sign: "an invite mechanism's conversion rate responds to design in measurable, repeatable ways." It will not sign: "word of mouth that leaves no referral token belongs inside K" — that, it argues, is unfalsifiable and unmanageable.

The loop school — Brian Balfour, Casey Winters and the growth-model tradition that grew up around them — holds that K is an over-compression. The correct unit of analysis is the whole loop: retention feeds frequency, frequency feeds exposure, exposure feeds sends, sends feed activation, and activation feeds retention again. It will sign: "any viral number that is not a function of retention is a number about a moment, not about a system." It will not sign: "you can manage a growth team by setting a K target," which it regards as the single most reliable way to get an invite surface over-optimised and a retention problem ignored.

The diffusion school — Frank Bass's 1969 model of new-product adoption, with its coefficient of external influence p and internal influence q, and behind it the Ehrenberg-Bass marketing-science tradition — holds that spread is driven overwhelmingly by category penetration and the size of the already-exposed population, and that internal word of mouth cannot bootstrap itself without substantial external seeding. It draws additional support from Duncan Watts and Peter Dodds's 2007 simulation work, which found that large cascades are usually the product of a susceptible population rather than of exceptional individuals. It will sign: "reach buys you the p without which your q has nothing to work on." It will not sign: "seeding a few influential users is an efficient substitute for broad reach."

The product-as-distribution school holds that virality is structural: it lives in what the product does, not in a feature bolted onto it. A messaging product is viral because it is useless alone; a document-approval product is viral because approval requires a second party; a solitary-use product is not viral and no incentive will make it so. It will sign: "you cannot add K to a product whose core use is single-player." It will not sign: "incentives create virality," conceding only that incentives can accelerate a loop that structurally exists.

The camps are not reconcilable by a tidy synthesis, and pretending otherwise is how teams end up with a growth strategy that is internally contradictory. Where they collide hardest: whether K is forecastable or merely observable, whether incentivised referral is virality at all, and whether the marginal rupee belongs in the loop or in reach. We return to those collisions, steelmanned, in section 10.

3. Mechanics in depth: decomposing the number that everybody quotes

The textbook form is K = i × c, invites sent per user multiplied by the conversion rate per invite. It is correct and nearly useless for diagnosis, because both terms are composites and the composites move independently. Expert practice decomposes K into five multiplicative factors, each of which has a different owner, a different intervention set and a different decay curve:

K = e × s × m × d × a, where e is the share of active users who actually reach the invite surface in the window (an exposure problem, owned by the core product team's placement decisions); s is the share of exposed users who send at least one invitation (a motivation problem); m is the mean number of invitations per sender, conditional on sending (a friction and channel problem); d is the share of invitations delivered and opened (a channel problem, and largely outside the company's control); and a is the share of opened invitations that reach the activation bar (a recipient-side problem — product value legibility, onboarding, and, crucially, whether the recipient is still susceptible at all).

Run Jeevika Learning's collapse through the decomposition and the diagnosis writes itself. In the September 2025 quarter: e = 0.68, s = 0.31, m = 9.9 (a study-group invitation broadcast into a class WhatsApp group counts as one invitation per recipient), d = 0.62, a = 0.40. The product is 0.68 × 0.31 × 9.9 × 0.62 × 0.40 = 0.518, the 0.52 the team had reported. In the March 2026 quarter: e = 0.66, s = 0.29, m = 9.4, d = 0.58, a = 0.20 — giving 0.66 × 0.29 × 9.4 × 0.58 × 0.20 = 0.209. Four of the five factors are essentially unchanged, well inside quarter-to-quarter noise. Senders are still being exposed; they are still sending; they are still sending roughly as many. The entire collapse is in a, which halved. That is not a feature going stale. That is the recipient pool running out of people who do not already have the app.

Two further pieces of machinery separate a fluent practitioner from a competent one. The first is the amplification factor. For K below 1, the descendants of a seed cohort form a decaying geometric series summing to 1/(1−K), so Jeevika's loop at 0.52 was turning every paid user into 2.08 users and at 0.21 turns them into 1.27 — the practical consequence being that Jeevika's effective acquisition cost rose from ₹103 to ₹169 per user without the Meta auction moving a rupee. Read that way, K is not a growth engine; it is a discount rate on paid acquisition, and the relevant comparison is never K against 1 but the fully loaded cost of a viral user against the fully loaded cost of a bought one.

The second is cycle time, T, and the way it interacts with retention in a manner most treatments skip. If K exceeds 1, users compound as N(t) = N₀ × Kt/T, and the doubling time is T × ln2 / ln K: a loop with K = 1.15 and a six-day cycle doubles in roughly thirty days, while the same K with a seventy-day cycle doubles in about eleven months, by which time the market will have voted on something else. If K is below 1, T governs how long the amplification takes to arrive: about 93% of the 1/(1−K) multiple lands within four cycle times. Jeevika, at six days, banks its amplification inside a month. Jaideep, whose counterparty-to-new-workspace cycle has a median of 71 days, waits nine months for the same proportion — which is why a board asking for results by Q4 should treat the two loops as different instruments even at an identical coefficient.

The under-discussed interaction is this: a generation that churns before it reproduces does not reproduce. If mean user lifetime is shorter than the cycle time, the loop is subcritical no matter what the invite surface does, because the mathematics assumes every activated user survives to be exposed again. The honest formulation for a subscription or habit product is a per-period coefficient multiplied by expected periods of survival: Jeevika's per-month figure of 0.09, across a mean active lifetime of 5.5 months, gives a lifetime K of 0.495. It follows — and this is the loop school's strongest single point — that a retention improvement raises K without anyone touching the invite surface at all, and that the cheapest available virality work at most companies is not invite-surface work.

4. Conditions, stated as testable claims

Virality is not a universal property that some products have more of. It requires five conditions, each of which can be tested before a rupee of engineering is committed. Applied honestly to Kavya's and Anirudh's situations, they explain why the same decision framework produces opposite recommendations.

C1: the product generates an artefact or an obligation that crosses a boundary as part of normal use. Jaideep passes emphatically — an approval request is, by construction, a demand made of someone outside the account, and the product does not function without it. Jeevika passes weakly: a study group is a real artefact, but preparation for a competitive examination is fundamentally solitary and the group is optional. Test it by asking what fraction of the core job-to-be-done is impossible alone.

C2: the recipient's benefit is legible before signup. Jaideep's counterparty knows exactly why the link arrived; the document is in front of them. Jeevika's recipient receives an invitation to install an app that they might have needed anyway. Test it by measuring open-to-activation conversion for cold recipients with no prior brand exposure.

C3: the reachable graph is materially larger than current penetration. Jaideep passes: its customers' counterparty sets are wide, heterogeneous and mostly untouched. Jeevika fails in its core districts, which is the whole story of section 3, and passes in districts it has not yet seeded. Test it with penetration by geography and by cohort of the recipient's own contact graph, not with a national average.

C4: the cycle closes fast relative to the decision horizon and to user lifetime. Jeevika passes at six days; Jaideep fails at seventy-one, which does not kill the mechanism but does mean it cannot be the answer to a board question due in two quarters.

C5: the marginal cost of serving a viral user is near zero. Both passed historically; Jeevika's new AI doubt-solver, at roughly ₹38 per active user per month of inference, is quietly falsifying C5 for them, which is a genuinely new development treated in section 5.

Where the idea becomes actively misleading is worth naming directly. For high-consideration, low-frequency purchases — a home loan, a hospital's radiology system — the interval between one user's adoption and their next opportunity to influence anyone is measured in years, and a coefficient computed over ninety days is arithmetic applied to noise. For supply-constrained businesses, a K above 1 is a fulfilment crisis rather than a triumph. And in regulated categories, the invite mechanism may be legally constrained in ways the model does not see at all.

5. Hard edge cases

Two-sided products: one K is always the wrong number

In a marketplace or any two-sided product, four coefficients exist, not one: supply inviting supply, supply inviting demand, demand inviting supply, demand inviting demand. Epidemiology solved this problem long ago with the next-generation matrix, and the system's true reproduction number is the dominant eigenvalue of that matrix — not the average of its entries, and certainly not the larger diagonal term. The practical consequence is startling and almost never modelled in growth decks: a system in which neither side alone is self-sustaining can still be supercritical overall, purely through cross-side transmission.

Regulated categories: the invite surface is not always yours to design

Indian product teams meet this sooner than most. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 reshapes the oldest trick in the viral playbook — uploading a user's contact book to find and message their friends — because the people in that contact book are data principals who never consented to anything. The defensible pattern is on-device matching with hashed identifiers and a user-initiated share rather than a server-side contact upload, which typically costs a chunk of m and buys a durable position. Financial-services and insurance distribution sit under referral rules from the RBI, SEBI and IRDAI that restrict who may be compensated for introducing a customer and how; a "refer a friend and both get ₹500" mechanic that is unremarkable for a gaming app can constitute unlicensed distribution for an insurance product. Multi-level referral structures — where a referrer earns from their referrals' referrals — run into the Prize Chits and Money Circulation Schemes (Banning) Act, 1978, and the fact that a growth team invented the scheme rather than a fraudster does not change its legal characterisation. The expert reflex is to route any incentivised loop past counsel before it is built, not after it works.

Borrowed channels: the platform can revoke your distribution

Almost every viral loop rides a channel the company does not own. India's dominant invite channel is WhatsApp, which in 2018 restricted message forwarding to five chats — a public-safety response to misinformation, entirely reasonable, and instantly a step-change in the economics of every broadcast-style invite mechanic in the country. The same has happened repeatedly elsewhere: platform notification channels that were open and then were not, SMS routes reshaped by TRAI's DLT registration regime, app-store policies on incentivised installs, and mobile-OS changes to identifier availability that broke referral attribution wholesale. The tell is unmistakable in hindsight and easy to miss live: K step-changes on a date on which the team shipped nothing.

Hardware and physical goods: long cycles, hard ceilings

Jayanti Instruments, a Pune manufacturer of connected water-quality and haemoglobin testing devices sold to small-town clinics and pathology labs, has a genuine viral surface — every printed patient report carries the device's mark and a QR code, and a clinic that sees a neighbouring clinic's report is a warm lead. But the cycle from first exposure to an installed second device runs about 150 days through demonstration, financing and delivery, and the coefficient sits near 0.11. More importantly, Jayanti Instruments cannot want a K above 1: its contract manufacturer's committed capacity is 1,400 units a quarter, and a supercritical loop would convert enthusiasm into a fourteen-week backlog and cancellations. For hardware, the discipline is to treat virality as a lead-generation discount on a sales-led motion, never as a growth engine, and to model the loop against capacity rather than against ambition.

AI-native products: virality that costs money per user, forever

The classic viral arithmetic silently assumes a marginal serving cost of approximately zero — the assumption that made Hotmail's footer rational. AI-native products break it. Jeevika's doubt-solver answers a photographed question with a worked solution, and each solution card is itself a share-ready artefact; the loop is elegant and the artefact is genuinely useful, which is exactly the structural virality the product-as-distribution school approves of. It also costs roughly ₹38 per active user per month in inference against a subscription taken up by 3.1% of actives. On free-tier users, the loop therefore accelerates a negative contribution margin: doubling K doubles the rate at which the company acquires users it loses money on. The correct move is not to suppress the loop but to gate the expensive capability behind the activation or payment step, so that virality recruits into the cheap surface and monetisation happens before the costly one. Teams that do not do this discover that a supercritical loop on a negative-margin product is indistinguishable from a bug in the billing system.

The organisational seam

The invite surface almost always sits inside a moment owned by a core product team, while K is owned by a growth team, while the incentive budget sits with finance and the legal exposure sits with counsel. What mature companies actually do — as distinct from what their conference talks describe — is arbitrate this with a standing rule about which team owns the moment and which owns the mechanism, a shared definition of activation written down and version-controlled, and an explicit prohibition on K as a team OKR. Where K becomes an OKR, it gets optimised: activation bars quietly loosen, windows quietly lengthen, and the number goes up while the business does not. A leader who has seen this twice recognises the smell immediately — a rising coefficient with a flat blended acquisition cost.

6. Nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

K is a property of the graph, not of the product

The tell is a feature that ships unchanged into a new state or district and returns a coefficient two or three times different. The obvious reading — that the new market is "less viral," or that localisation is poor — is usually wrong. What differs is penetration and network topology: an examination-preparation product entering a district where 4% of aspirants already have it converts invitations at a rate it will never see again once penetration passes 30%. The expert consequence is that K must always be stamped with a geography and a penetration level, and that a national average is a weighted blend of markets in entirely different regimes.

The mean conceals a distribution that determines the outcome

Epidemiologists model transmission with a negative binomial rather than a Poisson precisely because dispersion matters as much as the mean: with the same average, a highly dispersed process produces mostly dead ends and rare explosions. The tell is week-to-week instability in K that no product change explains, plus a top decile of senders carrying more than 80% of invitations. The obvious reading — "we have power users, let us target them" — is not wrong so much as incomplete: high dispersion also means the extinction probability of any given seed is high, so a portfolio of many small seeds behaves very differently from one large one, and a forecast built on the mean will be confidently wrong in both directions.

Retention sits upstream of virality, not beside it

The tell is a coefficient that rises a month after an onboarding or habit fix that nobody connected to growth. Because exposure requires survival, lifetime K is a per-period rate multiplied by expected lifetime, and the second term is usually the softer one. The obvious reading treats retention and virality as two lines in a growth model to be optimised independently; the expert reading treats the viral coefficient as partly a restatement of retention, and audits every claimed viral win for whether it was actually a retention win.

The denominator that matters is unique reachable recipients, not invitations

Jeevika's data shows the first invitation to a given phone number converting at 31%, the second at 12%, the third at 4%. As a loop matures, the share of invitations landing on already-invited people climbs, and aggregate conversion falls even though the per-recipient conversion curve has not moved at all. The tell is a widening gap between invitations sent and unique recipients reached. The obvious reading blames the creative or the reward; the correct instrument is a suppression list and a measurement of conversion by invitation ordinality.

Clustering shrinks the reachable graph faster than penetration suggests

Social graphs are not random: aspirants preparing for the same examination know each other, resellers in a town know each other, and the counterparties of a logistics firm cluster around the same corridors. In a clustered graph, a sender's contacts overlap heavily with contacts already reached by earlier senders, so the effective susceptible pool per invitation falls much faster than overall market penetration implies. A product at 12% national penetration can already be at 60% penetration inside the clusters that its early adopters inhabit. The tell is a collapse in conversion while national penetration still looks trivially small.

Attribution is generous by construction, and the generosity compounds

Referral-token attribution credits the loop with anyone who arrives carrying a token, including the many who were already going to arrive and for whom the link was simply the most convenient door. The tell is referral-attributed installs growing steadily while blended acquisition cost is flat. The obvious reading is that referral is working; the expert reading is that nothing has been established until a holdout has run, and the cost of the holdout — a few weeks of foregone growth on a slice of traffic — is far below the cost of a year of roadmap allocated on a number inflated by 60%.

Incentives select the sender as well as the recipient

Everyone knows that cash incentives can attract low-quality recipients. Fewer notice that they also change who sends: an unincentivised loop is dominated by enthusiasts recommending something they value, while a cash loop recruits senders motivated by the cash, whose recommendations carry less social weight and whose own retention is frequently worse than the base. The tell is the referred cohort's retention falling at the same time as the referring cohort's retention falls. The remedy is rarely to remove incentives entirely; it is to shift them from cash toward product-denominated value that only a genuine user can use.

A loop slower than the churn cycle cannot compound, whatever K says

If mean active lifetime is four months and the cycle time is five, the second generation is largely made up of people whose parents are already gone. The tell is a healthy-looking coefficient with cohort curves that stubbornly refuse to show the predicted second-generation bump. The obvious reading is that attribution is leaky; the correct diagnostic is to plot the distribution of cycle times against the survival curve and check what proportion of the loop closes inside the survival window.

A coefficient above 1 is a liability as often as an asset

Supercritical growth arrives with support load, fraud, moderation burden, fulfilment strain and, for AI products, an inference bill, all of which scale with the same exponent as the users. The tell is a team celebrating compounding installs while refund rates, support backlog and cost-to-serve climb quietly in a different function's dashboard. The obvious reading is that these are execution problems to be fixed later; the expert reading is that they are the reason most companies that briefly exceed 1 do not enjoy it.

The right comparison is never K against 1

The question that matters is whether the fully loaded cost per viral user — incentive spend, fraud losses, support load and amortised engineering, divided by incremental activated users — beats paid acquisition cost on a lifetime-value-adjusted basis. A K of 0.22 obtained for ₹41 per user against a paid cost of ₹214 is a superb business; a K of 0.6 obtained for ₹260 per user with 40% worse retention is a subsidy programme with a growth chart attached. The tell is a team that can quote its coefficient to two decimals and cannot quote its cost per viral user at all.

7. How this differs across product types and stages

The arithmetic does not change across contexts; four things do. What changes is the graph the product sits in, the cycle time, the activation bar that makes a conversion real, and who bears the cost of the marginal user. Almost every claimed difference between consumer and enterprise virality reduces to one of those four, and it is worth saying plainly that the differences people most often assert — that B2B products "cannot" be viral, or that consumer virality is "about emotion" — are not real differences, just different values of the same parameters.

In consumer products the graph is dense and cheap to traverse, cycle times run in days, and the binding constraint is almost always saturation within clusters. In B2B and enterprise the graph is thin but the nodes are enormously valuable: a single counterparty conversion at Jaideep is worth ₹1.1 lakh of annual contract value, so a coefficient of 0.16 is worth more per point than a consumer coefficient of 0.5. Enterprise introduces a structural obstacle that consumer does not have — procurement, security review and IT approval sit between activation and adoption, effectively adding a second, slower conversion step that no invite-surface change can remove. The expert move in enterprise is therefore to measure account-level virality and seat-level expansion as two separate quantities: seat expansion inside an existing customer is revenue expansion, not virality, and blending the two is how enterprise growth teams talk themselves into believing they have a loop when they have an upsell.

Platforms and marketplaces demand the matrix treatment of section 5, and additionally require the operator to weight conversions by scarcity: a referral on the constrained side is worth several times a referral on the abundant side, and a blended coefficient hides precisely the allocation decision that matters. Hardware imposes capacity ceilings and long cycles, and the honest framing is lead generation rather than compounding. AI products are the first category in which the loop's success can be financially adverse, and they are also the first in which the shared artefact can be generated by the product rather than by the user, which raises a question the field has not settled: whether an artefact the user did not author carries the social credibility that made shared artefacts convert in the first place.

By stage, the estimate itself changes character. At seed stage, with a few thousand users, K is statistically noisy, the activation bar is usually still moving, and a handful of enthusiastic early adopters can carry the entire estimate — yet this is when a real loop matters most, because paid acquisition is least affordable. At growth stage, the number stabilises and becomes forecastable for roughly a quarter at a time, which is the window in which the coefficient school's claims are most defensible. At scale, K declines structurally through saturation and invite fatigue, and the discipline shifts from raising it to defending it and to re-measuring it by market rather than nationally. At maturity, even 0.05 is worth defending in absolute rupees — five percent of a very large acquisition budget is a real number — but it should stop being reported as a headline metric, because a figure that small invites more misinterpretation than it resolves.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Jaideep Systems: an argument about definitions, settled by a holdout

Kavya refused to arbitrate between 0.34 and 0.04 and instead ran the only experiment that could settle it. Over nine weeks from mid-February 2026, 6,200 external counterparties were randomly assigned: the control arm received the existing frictionless signing link, the treatment arm was required to create a free identity before signing. The results were unambiguous in both directions. Self-serve workspace creation among treated counterparties rose from 0.40% to 1.04% on a twelve-month basis — at 41 counterparties per workspace per year, an account-level incremental coefficient moving from 0.164 to 0.43. Across 2,600 workspaces that is 683 additional self-serve workspaces a year at roughly ₹1.1 lakh of annual contract value, or about ₹7.5 crore of incremental ARR acquired at a marginal cost near zero against a sales-led logo cost of ₹1.9 lakh. And the counterparty completion rate for the signature itself — the job Jaideep's customers actually pay for — fell from 94% to 88%.

Six percentage points of completion on the core promise is not a rounding error; it is the sort of number that shows up in renewal conversations. What made the decision tractable was a segment cut nobody had asked for. Counterparties who had signed three or more documents in ninety days — repeat counterparties — were 23% of counterparty volume but 61% of self-serve conversions, and their completion rate fell only 1.5 points under the identity requirement, because they had already decided the product was part of their working life. Requiring identity only of repeat counterparties captures roughly 61% of the viral upside, about ₹4.6 crore of incremental ARR, at a quarter of the friction cost.

Jeevika Learning: a decay correctly diagnosed

Anirudh's decomposition had already located the collapse in recipient-side activation. The confirmation came from geography. Re-cut by district, the March 2026 coefficient was 0.14 in Jeevika's twelve oldest districts, where penetration of the serious-aspirant population exceeded 34%, and 0.38 in eleven districts seeded after June 2025. The feature was not stale; the graph was full. Two changes followed. A suppression rule stopped third and subsequent invitations to the same number, which raised conversion per invitation without reducing unique reach. And the activation bar was redefined from "installed and opened" to "completed one mock test," which lowered the reported coefficient by about a fifth and raised its correlation with subscription revenue enough that the finance team stopped disputing it.

Jayanti Circle: a coefficient above 1, and what happened next

Jayanti Circle, a Jaipur social-commerce application through which home-based resellers sold apparel and household goods into their own WhatsApp networks, is the cautionary case, and it is instructive precisely because nothing about its early numbers looked wrong. Between October 2024 and January 2025 it measured a viral coefficient of 1.4 on a referral mechanic paying ₹120 to each side on a converted referral, and added 480,000 installs in fourteen weeks. In week fifteen the curve rolled over. The post-mortem found three causes operating at once. Saturation: the reseller graph in the seeded districts reached about 26% penetration, and the ceiling for a loop at K = 1.4 is 1 − 1/1.4, or 28.6% of the reachable graph — the growth stopped almost exactly where the arithmetic said it would. Fraud: 31% of referral-attributed installs traced to roughly 2,900 device clusters, and the incentive liability carried on the balance sheet reached ₹4.2 crore. Quality: day-30 retention of the referred cohort was 6% against 24% for organic. The recovery took two quarters and looked nothing like a growth campaign. The cash incentive was withdrawn entirely. The company built a shareable storefront page — the reseller's own catalogue, which she already wanted to circulate — making the artefact the invitation. The coefficient settled at 0.29, referred-cohort day-30 retention came in at 21% against 24% organic, the fully loaded cost per viral user was ₹41 against a paid cost of ₹268, and blended acquisition cost fell 17% over two quarters. The company grew more slowly and, for the first time, kept what it grew.

9. Failure modes, their early warnings and the cost of catching them late

The pattern across all six is that the headline coefficient is the last thing to move. By the time K visibly falls, the underlying cause has typically been operating for two quarters. This is the strongest practical argument for instrumenting the five factors separately from day one: the decomposition is an early-warning system, whereas the coefficient is a post-mortem.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Four disagreements in this field are live, held by serious people, and not resolvable by appealing to a framework. Each is set out here in the form its strongest advocate would recognise.

Is K forecastable, or only observable? The coefficient school's position rests on real evidence: within a stable market and a stable penetration band, invite-surface conversion responds to design changes with reasonable reproducibility, and teams that run structured experiments do move the number reliably. The loop school's counter rests on equally real evidence: published viral forecasts miss badly and asymmetrically, because the coefficient is a function of penetration, channel policy and retention, all of which drift. What would have to be true for the coefficient school to be wrong: that the residual variance in K after controlling for design changes is dominated by graph and channel factors rather than product factors — which is exactly what Jeevika's decomposition shows, and exactly what a company in a young, unsaturated market would not yet see.

Do incentives create virality or corrode it? The case for incentives is that they solve a coordination problem: a genuinely useful product often fails to spread because nobody has a reason to act today, and a reward converts latent goodwill into a dated action — with the further evidence that several of the most-cited viral programmes in software history were incentivised. The case against is that incentives substitute extrinsic for intrinsic motivation, select worse senders and worse recipients, create fraud surface and accrue liability, and mask whether the product spreads at all. What would settle it in a given company is narrow and measurable: compare retention and lifetime value of the incentivised referred cohort against the unincentivised referred cohort from the same period. What would have to be true for the pro-incentive position to be wrong is that this gap persists after controlling for recipient type — which at Jayanti Circle it emphatically did, and at other companies it does not.

Should unattributed word of mouth count? The token-based camp argues that a metric you cannot attribute is a metric you cannot manage, and that including a survey-derived estimate of informal word of mouth turns K into an unfalsifiable number that will be inflated by whoever has an interest in inflating it. The diffusion camp argues that the token-based number systematically understates spread, sometimes by multiples, because the majority of real recommendation happens in conversations that leave no link — and that Bass-style estimation from adoption curves, or well-run attribution surveys, capture something the telemetry structurally cannot. Both are right about their own failure mode. The practical resolution most sophisticated teams adopt is to maintain two numbers with different names and never to add them.

Is engineered virality worth the investment at all? The marketing-science position — associated with the Ehrenberg-Bass tradition and given empirical support by Watts and Dodds's finding that large cascades depend more on the susceptibility of the population than on the influence of individuals — is that most companies would obtain more growth per rupee from broad reach than from loop engineering, and that the visible successes of viral design suffer from severe survivorship bias. The growth-engineering counter is that reach is rented and loops are owned, that the compounding discount on acquisition cost is permanent while media buying is not, and that the comparison should be made on a multi-year basis. The honest state of the evidence is that the diffusion camp is probably right for products with weak structural virality and the engineering camp probably right for products with strong structural virality, which returns the argument to the product-as-distribution school's test and leaves it unresolved for everyone in the middle — which is most companies.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this topic quotes a coefficient. Someone who has internalised it does five things differently, and they are recognisable in a meeting within about ten minutes.

They never state K without its four stamps — population, window, activation bar, counterfactual — and they visibly flinch when someone else does. They reach for the decomposition before the headline, so that their first question about a change in the number is which factor moved, not what the number now is. They treat a holdout as a routine cost of doing business rather than as an unusual exercise requiring approval, because they have priced the alternative. They discuss cycle time and retention in the same breath as the coefficient, having understood that a loop is a system with a clock and a survival curve rather than a multiplier. And they hold the number lightly: they expect it to decay, they re-measure it by market, and they are entirely comfortable telling a board that a coefficient which was true in September is not evidence about March. The deepest marker is the last one. A practitioner is trying to raise K. An expert is trying to work out what K is currently a measurement of, and whether the answer still supports the decision it was originally used to justify.

12. What each protagonist decides

Kavya Raghunathan takes the segmented path. Jaideep Systems will require an identity only from repeat counterparties — those who have signed three or more documents in ninety days — capturing an estimated ₹4.6 crore of incremental self-serve ARR for a 1.5-point cost to completion in that segment rather than a 6-point cost across all of it. She commits to reporting the mechanism as an incremental, holdout-derived account-level coefficient of about 0.43 in the treated segment, with the twelve-month cycle-time caveat stated in the same sentence, and she declines to use Tanmay's 0.34 at all, on the grounds that a number containing sales-sourced logos is not a measurement of the product. Sunayana's 0.04 she keeps as an internal floor. Sales gets a written commitment that completion rate in the treated segment becomes a tracked guardrail with a rollback threshold.

Anirudh Bhatia does not rebuild the loop. He redeploys it: the same feature, unchanged, into eleven newly seeded districts where it measures 0.38, while in the twelve saturated districts he stops treating it as an acquisition lever at all and repurposes the study-group surface for engagement, where its contribution is real and no longer fraudulent to report. He cuts the referral incentive budget from ₹6.4 crore to ₹2.1 crore and moves the difference into vernacular reach in districts Jeevika has never touched — conceding, in effect, the diffusion school's point that a loop with nothing to work on is not a strategy. And he changes what the company reports: not a national coefficient, but a coefficient by penetration decile, with a stated expectation that each district's number will decay toward 0.15 within five quarters of seeding, and a plan that assumes it.

Question one: Kavya's 0.43 and Sunayana's 0.04 are both defensible measurements of the same mechanism. If you were the board member hearing only one of them, what would you need to ask to know which one you were being shown — and what does it say about the metric that this question is necessary at all?

Question two: Jayanti Circle's loop worked exactly as the arithmetic predicted, right up to the ceiling the arithmetic also predicted. Was the failure the incentive, the fraud, the saturation, or the decision to treat a coefficient of 1.4 as evidence of an engine rather than as evidence of an unexploited pool? Which of those would you have caught in week three?

Question three: Anirudh is redeploying a loop he knows will decay to roughly 0.15 in every market he seeds. At what coefficient does a viral mechanism stop earning its maintenance cost — and who in a company should be allowed to make that call, given that the growth team is the one least able to make it disinterestedly?

13. Going deeper

  1. Product-led growth — the operating model in which the product, rather than a sales team, carries acquisition; virality is its acquisition engine, and PLG is where the Jaideep decision about counterparty identity is really being made.
  2. Network effects — the value-side counterpart to virality's acquisition side; understanding why a product gets better as it grows explains why some loops have rising rather than decaying conversion, and unlocks the analysis of defensibility.
  3. Case: Dropbox — the canonical worked example of a loop that briefly exceeded 1, with real numbers on incentive design, storage economics and the eventual decay; read it after this page and the arithmetic will already be familiar.
  4. Referral programme design — the operational layer beneath the coefficient: reward structure, two-sided versus one-sided payout, fraud control, suppression rules and the legal constraints that decide what is buildable in Indian regulated categories.
  5. Growth loops vs funnels — the structural argument behind the loop school in section 2; it reframes virality as one compounding loop among several and explains why K alone is an inadequate management object.
  6. Building a growth model — where K becomes an input rather than a headline; the spreadsheet discipline that forces cycle time, retention and saturation into the same forecast and exposes coefficient-only reasoning.
  7. Acquisition channels and economics — the comparison set that gives K its meaning, since the coefficient is only ever valuable relative to the cost of the paid alternative it displaces.
  8. Activation and onboarding optimisation — the single factor that collapsed at Jeevika; recipient-side activation is where most viral coefficient is won or lost, and it is owned by a different team than the one that reports K.
  9. Engagement loops and habit — the mechanism that determines exposure frequency, and therefore how many chances a user gets to invite anyone before they churn.
  10. Retention strategy — upstream of everything here: lifetime K is a per-period rate multiplied by survival, so the cheapest available virality work at most companies is retention work that nobody labels as such.
